section_summary: This section follows American and British oil companies’ efforts to negotiate the application of Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially sales quotas, compulsory oil stocks, refining rights and price controls. Embassy reports describe the talks with Japanese officials, related concern over the Manchurian oil monopoly, and a possible oil monopoly in Korea. The section also contains duplicate telegram copies, filing notes, newspaper clippings and a broader survey of world petroleum production and consumption.

subfiles.title: Telegram on confidential oil-company communications
subfiles.about: Walden and Parker seek cautious use of official coded channels during talks with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays their request to send important confidential messages through State Department channels and asks for instructions.

subfiles.title: Instruction on coded communications
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether British oil interests receive equivalent coded-message service.
subfiles.summary: Dundas has been sent the message; the Embassy is asked urgently about British practice.

subfiles.title: Conditions for transmitting company messages
subfiles.about: The Department sets conditions for carrying highly confidential Standard-Vacuum messages.
subfiles.summary: Messages must be paraphrased; the company pays charges and accepts transmission risks.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter to Dundas on message transmission
subfiles.about: The Department explains limited confidential communications assistance during the Japanese oil talks.
subfiles.summary: It confirms Walden and Parker's warning about cable security and describes the Department's conditional willingness to transmit important messages.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Tokyo telegram of January 7
subfiles.about: Walden and Parker request careful cable handling during negotiations.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of the telegram on use of official codes.

subfiles.title: British Embassy practice on coded oil messages
subfiles.about: The British Embassy permits oil interests limited use of its official codes.
subfiles.summary: Grew says British permission depends on avoiding abuse and has not required Foreign Office approval.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Tokyo telegram of January 8
subfiles.about: British coded-message practice is reported again.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of the British Embassy telegram.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch 1090
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to developments in enforcing Japan's petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Points to despatch 1090 on the Petroleum Industry Law.

subfiles.title: Extract on petroleum law enforcement
subfiles.about: Japanese officials discuss provisional import plans and sales quotas with foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: After rejecting foreign requests to change the law or abolish stockholding, officials offer provisional 1935 sales quotas. Standard-Vacuum submits conditional information while deciding whether business in Japan remains viable.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch 1092
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to the petroleum question in Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Notes a conversation with the Netherlands Minister about security of the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Opening of talks at the Tokyo Club
subfiles.about: American and British oil representatives begin talks with Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: The first meeting was cordial; Embassy officials did not attend.

subfiles.title: Request for progress report on oil talks
subfiles.about: The Department requests a brief update on the talks.
subfiles.summary: Asks for progress to date unless reporting would be inexpedient.

subfiles.title: Dundas acknowledges coded-message arrangement
subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum accepts the Department's limits on forwarding urgent messages.
subfiles.summary: Dundas promises rare use, accepts paraphrasing and offers reimbursement.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch 1117
subfiles.about: An internal note highlights details in Grew's oil-situation report.
subfiles.summary: Flags Kurusu's remarks about Hashimoto and the report's Korea monopoly rumor.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1117
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports joint representations, Japanese responses and a rumored Korea oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: American and British Embassy officers jointly pressed Japan over the Petroleum Industry Law. Kurusu suggested that officials might discuss quotas, refining and stockholding with visiting company leaders, prompting them to travel from Shanghai. Grew also addresses coordination with Standard-Vacuum and reports a possible refinery and eventual sales monopoly in Korea.

subfiles.title: American Embassy paper on petroleum law
subfiles.about: The Embassy states American concerns over quotas, refining and stockholding.
subfiles.summary: Wide official powers and uncertain future sales make further American investment difficult to judge.

subfiles.title: British paper on petroleum law
subfiles.about: Britain details concerns that the Petroleum Industry Law could discriminate against British oil firms.
subfiles.summary: The paper questions annual operating plans, uncertain quotas, limits on refining and broad official intervention. It calls stockholding especially onerous and says Japanese explanations have not removed British concerns.

subfiles.title: Neville–Kurusu conversation on oil policy
subfiles.about: Kurusu discusses quotas, refining, stockholding and a possible meeting with Manchukuo's Hoshino.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu welcomes talks with Standard-Vacuum directors and promises equal treatment for foreign refineries. He expects adjustment of stockholding requirements because Japanese firms also struggle to comply. Neville adds observations on possible concessions and on Kurusu's proposed contact with Hoshino over the Manchurian monopoly.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of petroleum-law translations
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends English translations of Japanese and Manchurian petroleum laws.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck encloses the laws and a gazette correction, noting the translations are unofficial.

subfiles.title: Quinn thanks Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Standard Oil of California acknowledges receipt of petroleum-law translations.
subfiles.summary: Quinn thanks the Department for prompt assistance.

subfiles.title: Division note on negotiations and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: A staff note assesses embassy reporting and the possible four-month stock proposal.
subfiles.summary: The writer suggests awaiting Embassy initiative or asking for a brief update. The note distinguishes Manchukuo's treaty issues from Japan's oil controls and treats a four-month stock proposal as a company concession.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1126
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew outlines foreign oil companies' proposed changes and the opening Japanese talks.
subfiles.summary: American and British representatives developed proposals on trade guarantees, stocks, prices, refining, equipment, capital transfers and business restrictions. Talks opened at the Tokyo Club in a friendly atmosphere but produced no definite proposals. Grew also forwards clippings about a disputed report of Japanese interest in a Mexican oil field.

subfiles.title: Agenda for petroleum-law conversations
subfiles.about: Company representatives list issues for the talks.
subfiles.summary: Agenda covers trade guarantees, stocks, prices, exchange control, refining and business transfers.

subfiles.title: Mexican oil field offered for sale to Japanese firm
subfiles.about: A newspaper reports an alleged offer of Mexican oil fields to Nippon Oil.
subfiles.summary: The article links the reported offer to Japan's search for diverse crude supplies.

subfiles.title: Mexican sources deny oil field deal
subfiles.about: Mexican sources deny a reported Japanese oil-field purchase.
subfiles.summary: Officials call the alleged transaction impossible; observers cite Mexican efforts to preserve oil resources.

subfiles.title: Departmental press conference memorandum
subfiles.from: Division of Current Information; M. J. McDermott
subfiles.about: Under Secretary Phillips answers questions on Japan's oil talks and other current issues.
subfiles.summary: Phillips says the Department awaits results of company talks and has no precise recent report. He declines to discuss Manchukuo and also addresses Chahar and Brazil.

subfiles.title: Progress of oil negotiations
subfiles.about: Talks continue without concrete results.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials promise a written reply to company proposals the following week.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of world oil article
subfiles.about: The Department sends a world oil survey for background.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Garfias and Wetzel's article on petroleum consumption.

subfiles.title: World oil consumption next year to rival 1929
subfiles.from: V. R. Garfias and R. V. Wetzel
subfiles.about: An industry article surveys oil production, consumption and trade worldwide.
subfiles.summary: The article forecasts strong world petroleum production and consumption and reviews Iraq's new pipelines, Romanian difficulties, Japanese controls, Manchukuo's monopoly, Bahrain, Morocco, Trinidad and Mexico. Its final pages provide production, stock and consumption tables by country.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on unsatisfactory draft reply
subfiles.about: Japan's draft answer disappoints oil firms, and talks may pause until after the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Grew sees some basis for further discussion but reports that officials fear political repercussions from changing regulations during the Diet session.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Tokyo telegram of February 8
subfiles.about: A second copy reports Japan's draft answer and possible suspension of talks.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates the preceding telegram on delayed regulatory changes.

subfiles.title: Division note on despatch 1145
subfiles.about: A staff note evaluates Grew's report on oil negotiations.
subfiles.summary: No action is required; the report is recommended as useful reading.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1145
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew summarizes January talks on Japan's petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino explains the government's aims and discusses licensing, quotas, stockholding, prices, exchange control, refining and business transfers. Foreign representatives challenge the costs and uncertainty imposed by the law. The sides discuss a possible trade-percentage guarantee and flexible counting of stocks, but no concrete agreement emerges.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch 1136
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a report on Japan's Petroleum Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: Points to despatch 1136 on the law.

subfiles.title: Extract on Embassy representations
subfiles.about: The Embassy recounts joint December representations and Japan's invitation to oil-company directors.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu's response led the Embassy to perceive a more reasonable Japanese attitude.

subfiles.title: Division note on despatch 1168
subfiles.about: A staff note assesses the stalled negotiations reported in despatch 1168.
subfiles.summary: Talks ended with little agreement, though better terms might follow the Diet's adjournment.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch 1168
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports continued disagreement over quotas, stocks and prices.
subfiles.summary: Foreign companies submitted a memorandum of outstanding concerns on January 25 and discussed it with Japanese officials on January 30. Yoshino's February 4 draft reply refuses a guaranteed trade percentage or stockholding subsidies while promising flexible administration. The despatch continues beyond page 80.
